chapters.title: Chapter 1: ITR Basics: What, Why and Who Must File

lessons.title: Who Must File an ITR: Income Thresholds and Mandatory Filing Triggers

body.text: Zero tax does not mean zero filing. The law asks two separate questions: do you owe tax, and do you have to file? Plenty of Indians answer no to the first and yes to the second.

children.text: The most common line you hear during filing season is "my income is below ₹12 lakh, so I don't need to file." It is wrong for a large number of people. The ₹12 lakh figure is about tax payable after the rebate. Whether you must file is decided by a completely different set of tests. There are three of them, and triggering any one is enough.

All three tests live in Section 263 of the Income-tax Act, 2025 (Section 139(1) of the Income-tax Act, 1961). For returns of FY 2025-26 income filed in 2026, the 1961 Act provisions and Rule 12AB still govern, and the tests have carried over into the new Act in substance.
Test 1: Is Your Income Above the Basic Exemption Limit?

markDefs.definition: The level of income on which no tax is charged at all under the slab rates. It depends on your tax regime and, in the old regime, your age.

children.text: If your income for the year exceeds the
, you must file. Note what this limit is not: it is not the ₹12 lakh rebate threshold. The rebate removes the tax, but the income has still crossed the nil slab.

stats.label: Old Regime, Below 60
stats.context: If you have opted for the old regime

children.text: The Catch: Which Income Figure Do You Compare?

You compare your income before claiming deductions like 80C, 80D and 80CCD(1B), and before capital gains exemptions like Section 54 or 54EC. You cannot invest ₹1.5 lakh in ELSS and PPF to drag yourself below the limit and skip filing. The deduction reduces your tax, not your filing obligation.

body.title: What Counts in the Filing Test

columns.label: Already Reflected in the Income You Compare
points: Standard deduction on salary (₹75,000 new regime, ₹50,000 old regime)
Exempt salary allowances you are eligible for, like HRA in the old regime
Deduction for interest on a let-out property's home loan
Set-off of current year losses against other income

columns.label: Ignored: Add These Back Before Comparing
points: Section 80C investments: PPF, ELSS, EPF, life insurance, tuition fees
Capital gains exemptions under Sections 54, 54EC and 54F
The ₹1.25 lakh tax-free portion of long-term equity gains is not a deduction, so the full gain counts

body.title: Find the Filing-Test Income
body.prompt: Vikram, 35, works at a logistics firm in Ahmedabad and has opted for the old regime for FY 2025-26. His gross salary is ₹3,40,000. He invested ₹1,50,000 in PPF and ELSS. What income figure should he compare with the ₹2,50,000 basic exemption limit?
body.explanation: Gross salary of ₹3,40,000 less the old regime standard deduction of ₹50,000 gives ₹2,90,000. The ₹1,50,000 under Section 80C is ignored for the filing test. Since ₹2,90,000 exceeds ₹2,50,000, Vikram must file, even though after the 80C deduction his taxable income is only ₹1,40,000 and his tax is nil.

body.text: The rebate trap: Neha earns a salary of ₹7,50,000 at an IT firm in Kolkata and is in the new regime. After the ₹75,000 standard deduction, her income is ₹6,75,000. Her tax is fully wiped out by the rebate for income up to ₹12 lakh. But ₹6,75,000 is well above the ₹4,00,000 basic exemption limit, so filing is mandatory. Nil tax, compulsory return.

children.text: Test 2: Did You Cross a High-Value Transaction Trigger?

Some people with little or no taxable income still live a lifestyle, or run money through accounts, that the law wants on record. For them, filing is compulsory once they cross any of these triggers during the year, regardless of income.

body.caption: Mandatory Filing Triggers, Irrespective of Income (FY 2025-26)

cells: Deposits in one or more current accounts
More than ₹1 crore in aggregate
A trader routing sales cash through a current account at Axis Bank
Deposits in one or more savings accounts
₹50 lakh or more in aggregate
A family depositing proceeds from a property sale across two savings accounts
Foreign travel expenditure, for yourself or anyone else
More than ₹2 lakh in aggregate
Paying ₹2.4 lakh for a family trip to Bali
Electricity bills
More than ₹1 lakh in aggregate
Running two air conditioners through a Delhi summer in a large flat
TDS plus TCS deducted or collected
₹25,000 or more (₹50,000 or more for senior citizens)
A retiree whose FD interest carried ₹30,000 of TDS
Business turnover or sales
More than ₹60 lakh
A small garment shop in Surat
Gross receipts from a profession
More than ₹10 lakh
A freelance architect in Pune

body.text: Why the department notices: banks report large cash deposits, authorised dealers collect TCS on foreign tour packages and overseas remittances under LRS, and much of this flows into your AIS against your PAN. The filing obligation exists precisely because the department can already see the transaction.

body.title: Spot the Mandatory Filer
body.question: None of these four people has income above their basic exemption limit. Which one must still file an ITR for FY 2025-26?
options: Suresh, 62, new regime, pension of ₹3,20,000, who spent ₹1,80,000 on a trip to Dubai
Farah, a homemaker in Mumbai, with ₹2,00,000 FD interest and electricity bills totalling ₹1,20,000 for the year
Ishaan, a college student in Delhi, who earned ₹60,000 from freelance video editing
Kavita, 45, old regime, income of ₹2,40,000 on which ₹10,000 TDS was deducted
body.explanation: Farah's electricity bills crossed ₹1 lakh, which is a mandatory filing trigger regardless of income. Suresh's foreign travel spend of ₹1,80,000 is below the ₹2 lakh trigger and his pension is below ₹4 lakh. Ishaan's income is far below the limit and he crosses no trigger. Kavita's TDS of ₹10,000 is below the ₹25,000 trigger. Suresh, Ishaan and Kavita may still want to file, for example to claim a refund, but they are not required to.

body.title: Remember the TDS Trigger
body.textWithBlank: A 40-year-old must file an ITR if total TDS and TCS for the year is ₹___ or more, even if income is below the basic exemption limit.
body.explanation: The threshold is ₹25,000 of combined TDS and TCS for individuals below 60. For senior citizens aged 60 and above, it is ₹50,000.

children.text: Test 3: Do You Hold Any Asset Outside India?

A resident (and ordinarily resident) individual who, at any time during the year, holds an asset outside India, has a financial interest in a foreign entity, or has signing authority in a foreign bank account must file a return. Income does not matter. This catches far more people than it used to: US stocks bought through apps like INDmoney or Vested, RSUs and ESOPs from employers like Google, Microsoft or Amazon, and a bank account left open after studying abroad all count.

These assets are disclosed in Schedule FA, which is not available in ITR-1. Anyone in this bucket files ITR-2 or ITR-3. Leaving out a foreign asset can attract heavy penalties under the Black Money Act, so this is not a place to guess.

body.title: The Fresher With US Stocks
body.scenario: Divya, 23, joined a startup in Bengaluru in January 2026. Her salary for January to March 2026 is ₹2,70,000, and she is in the new regime. In November 2025, while still in college, she used ₹40,000 of her internship savings to buy Apple and Nvidia shares through a US investing app. Her employer deducted no TDS. Her friend says she has no reason to file, as her income is well below ₹4 lakh.
body.prompt: Does Divya have to file for FY 2025-26? If yes, what form will she need, and why?
body.modelAnswer: Yes, she must file. Her salary after the ₹75,000 standard deduction is ₹1,95,000, which is below the ₹4,00,000 limit, so she clears Test 1. She crosses no high-value trigger in Test 2. But she fails Test 3: as a resident, she held shares of US companies during the year, which are assets located outside India. That makes filing mandatory regardless of income. She cannot use ITR-1, because foreign assets must be disclosed in Schedule FA. She will file ITR-2, reporting her salary and her US holdings, plus any dividends received on them.

children.text: The One Group That Is Exempt: Seniors Aged 75 and Above

A resident senior citizen aged 75 or above can skip filing altogether, provided every condition is met. Their only income is pension and interest, the interest comes from the same specified bank that credits the pension, and they give that bank a declaration in Form 12BBA. The bank then computes the tax, including eligible deductions and the rebate, and deducts it as TDS. The relief sits in Section 263 of the Income-tax Act, 2025 (Section 194P of the 1961 Act).

body.label: 75+ Filing Exemption
body.value: Pension + interest from the same specified bank, with Form 12BBA
body.context: Rental income, capital gains, or interest from a second bank takes the senior out of this exemption, and the normal tests apply again.

body.caption: Answer in Order. One Yes Means You Must File.

cells: Is my income, before 80C, 80D and similar deductions, above my basic exemption limit?
File
Did I deposit more than ₹1 crore in current accounts, or ₹50 lakh or more in savings accounts?
File
Did I spend more than ₹2 lakh on foreign travel or more than ₹1 lakh on electricity?
File
Was my total TDS and TCS ₹25,000 or more (₹50,000 or more if 60+)?
File

File

File (ITR-2 or ITR-3)
All No? Am I owed a refund or carrying forward a loss?
Not mandatory, but file anyway (next lesson)

children.text: Under the Income-tax Act, 1961, which governs returns for FY 2025-26: the income test is in Section 139(1) itself, the foreign asset test is in its fourth proviso, the current account, foreign travel and electricity triggers are in its seventh proviso, and the turnover, professional receipts, TDS/TCS and savings deposit triggers are in Rule 12AB of the Income-tax Rules, 1962. The 75+ exemption is in Section 194P. Under the Income-tax Act, 2025, the return filing obligations and the 75+ exemption are consolidated into Section 263, applicable from Tax Year 2026-27.

body.title: One Family, Four Answers
body.scenario: The Iyer family lives in Chennai. For FY 2025-26: Ramesh, 76, receives a pension of ₹6,00,000 and FD interest of ₹1,50,000, both through SBI, and has submitted Form 12BBA to SBI. His wife Lakshmi, 70, in the new regime, earns ₹2,80,000 FD interest from Canara Bank, on which ₹28,000 TDS was deducted. Their son Arun, 32, earns a salary of ₹14,00,000 at Accenture. Arun's wife Meera, 30, is a homemaker with ₹1,20,000 in dividend income, and paid ₹2,60,000 from her own account for a family holiday in Switzerland.
body.prompt: Run each family member through the three tests. Who must file, who is exempt, and who should file even though they are not required to?
body.modelAnswer: Ramesh is exempt. He is over 75, his only income is pension and interest from the same specified bank, and he has submitted Form 12BBA, so SBI deducts his tax and he need not file. Lakshmi is not required to file. Her ₹2,80,000 income is below the ₹4,00,000 new regime limit, and her TDS of ₹28,000 is below the ₹50,000 trigger that applies to senior citizens. But she should file: her income is below the exemption limit, so no tax is due and the full ₹28,000 is refundable only through an ITR. Going forward, she can submit Form 15H to Canara Bank to stop the TDS. Arun must file, as ₹14,00,000 salary is far above ₹4,00,000. Meera must file. Her dividend income is below the limit, but she spent more than ₹2 lakh on foreign travel, which triggers mandatory filing on its own.

body.title: Run the Test on Yourself
steps: Add up your salary, interest, rent and gains for FY 2025-26, before any 80C or 80D deductions
Compare it with the basic exemption limit for your regime and age
Check your bank statements for total deposits into savings and current accounts
Add up any foreign travel spend, including tickets and hotels booked from India
Total your electricity bills for April 2025 to March 2026
Open your Form 26AS and add up TDS and TCS for the year
List any foreign shares, RSUs, ESOPs or overseas bank accounts you held at any point in the year

points: Whether you must file and whether you owe tax are two separate questions: a nil tax bill after the rebate does not remove the filing obligation

Test 1: file if income, computed before 80C, 80D and similar deductions, exceeds the basic exemption limit of ₹4 lakh in the new regime or ₹2.5 lakh, ₹3 lakh or ₹5 lakh in the old regime depending on age

Test 2: file if you cross any high-value trigger: current account deposits above ₹1 crore, savings deposits of ₹50 lakh or more, foreign travel above ₹2 lakh, electricity above ₹1 lakh, TDS plus TCS of ₹25,000 or more (₹50,000 for seniors), turnover above ₹60 lakh or professional receipts above ₹10 lakh
Test 3: residents holding any asset outside India, including US stocks, RSUs and foreign bank accounts, must file, using ITR-2 or ITR-3 with Schedule FA
Resident seniors aged 75 and above with only pension and interest from the same specified bank can skip filing by submitting Form 12BBA
These tests sit in Section 263 of the Income-tax Act, 2025 (Section 139(1) and Rule 12AB under the 1961 Act, which still govern FY 2025-26 returns)

body.text: This lesson is for educational purposes only and does not constitute tax advice. Exemption limits, transaction thresholds and filing conditions reflect the position for FY 2025-26 at the time of writing and can change through the Finance Act, the Income-tax Rules or CBDT notifications. Verify your specific situation on the Income Tax Department's portal or with a qualified tax professional.
